body.html: Note-taking apps work like warehouses — the more you store, the further you drift. ResearchTrace inverts that: it actively reads your library and delivers what matters.
ChatGPT gives you a sentence that looks right. ResearchTrace gives you a cited claim. Every conclusion is followed by ① ② ③ — three seconds back to the source.
Research happens in cycles, not chats. ResearchTrace delivers daily / weekly / monthly so you keep up without having to think about it — the only kind of leverage that scales.
ResearchTrace answers only against your library. Its foundation is the 2,000 documents you hold. That is the bright line between it and every general-purpose AI.

ov.kicker: EDITOR’S SYNTHESIS · synthesized by REPORTER AGENT · May 8, 23:47
ov.h1: The long-context contest: explicit memory compression vs end-to-end attention scaling, divergence intensifies.

body.html: Over the past 30 days this topic gathered 38 key claims and 412 pieces of evidence. Two main routes are diverging — Route A (DeepMind/Anthropic camp) argues for end-to-end attention window scaling; Route B (Microsoft Research/MemGPT camp) argues for external episodic memory in place of long windows. Curator's view: they are not mutually exclusive — H2 2026 will most likely converge on a «two-tier hybrid» architecture.

p1.html: Over the past 30 days, 412 pieces of literature evidence entered your library on long context. The most impactful: on May 7, DeepMind released Recurrent Memory Transformer v3, holding linear complexity at 2,097,152 tokens via recurrent compression1. The same week, Anthropic released Claude 3.5's needle-in-haystack at 200K — passing all 12 configurations at 99.4%2.

p2.html: Yet the alternative road implied by your LongMem save from Apr 173 — using an external memory module to «fake» long context — hasn't died. Microsoft Research's GraphRAG v0.4 experiment from May 34 shows that on 1M-token document QA, external memory + 8K window beat pure 200K on 11 of 17 metrics. The two routes win different task structures.

ov.h3: Three disagreements you should know about

li1.html: Compression-loss debate —— the RMT v3 paper claims ≤ 2.3% compression loss, but the Anthropic team points out the test set is biased toward narrative text, understating losses for code and tabular long-context5.

li2.html: Retrieval-eval debate —— is needle-in-haystack still valid? The HELM v3 team argues single-needle is too easy now — replace it with multi-needle + counterfactual needles6.

li3.html: Inference-cost debate —— your note from Apr 22 «The real cost of long windows» already pointed out: in production, 200K-context KV cache memory is 25× that of 8K — and no headline work has confronted this yet.

lede.html: Your two saves (RMT v3, MemGPT) represent two fundamentally different paradigms for handling «context that exceeds training length» — a distinction that produces order-of-magnitude cost differences in production. Worth your attention.

p1.html: RMT v3 uses recurrent compression to stuff entire context into a fixed-length hidden state, holding O(n) at 2M tokens1; MemGPT treats the model itself as an «operating system», using explicit memory scheduling (main context ↔ recall storage) to swap in information as needed2. The former is «implicit compression baked into weights»; the latter is «explicit run-time paging».

answer.h2: Three practical differences worth your attention

li1.html: Training vs inference-time opportunity cost: RMT v3 requires retraining or continued training of the base model1; MemGPT runs on frozen weights, in the same camp as the LongMem paper you saved on Apr 173.

li2.html: VRAM footprint: RMT v3's hidden-state memory is constant; MemGPT's main context is still bounded by standard KV cache — at 200K, KV cache reaches ~125 GB on a 70B model (your note #2204 from Apr 22 has the math).

li3.html: Failure modes: RMT v3 keeps compression loss ≤ 2.3% on narrative text, but Anthropic measured 14.7% on code and tabular tasks1; MemGPT's failure mode is «paging thrash» under bad scheduling — it needs engineering tuning.

p2.html: Worth noting: on May 3, Lilian Weng argued on her blog that even when the context fits, attention dilution still erodes multi-hop accuracy — hence «the promise of long windows is overstated in production»4. This indirectly supports MemGPT's engineering case.

curator.html: If you're building a conversational agent (multi-turn, long horizon), MemGPT gives you more control; if you're doing batch document analysis (one-shot long inputs), RMT v3's cost curve wins. Both will likely be unified under some two-tier hybrid architecture by 2026 H2.

body.html: Two heavy works landed in long-context this week: DeepMind's RMT v3 holds linear complexity at 2M tokens1; Anthropic reports Claude 3.5 at 99.4% accuracy on 200K needle tasks2. On the surface, technical breakthroughs; in practice, two conflicting routes — and evidence in your library already points to a third possibility (a two-tier hybrid).

h1.t: DeepMind releases Recurrent Memory Transformer v3
h1.d: Recurrent compression holds linear complexity at 2,097,152 tokens; outscores GPT-4-128K on LongBench-v2 by 11.2 pts.

h2.t: Claude 3.5 hits 99.4% on the 200K needle test
h2.d: Passes all 12 needle configurations; multi-hop subset at 73.1%.

h3.t: GraphRAG v0.4: 8K window + external memory wins 11 of 17
h3.d: Microsoft empirical: on long QA, «small window + strong retrieval» matches pure 200K.

p1.html: In the past 30 days, 412 pieces of literature evidence on long context entered your library. Most impactful: DeepMind's RMT v3 on May 71 and Anthropic's Claude 3.5 long-context report from the same week2. Both attack the same problem but along opposite paths — one uses compression to dodge the long-sequence cost, the other uses scaling to absorb it head-on.

p2.html: Your LongMem save from Apr 173 implies a third path: frozen base + external memory module. Microsoft's GraphRAG empirical study4 goes further: on 17 long-QA metrics, «small window + strong retrieval» matches pure 200K on 11. The real argument isn't «long vs short» — it's «where the information entropy is paid».

s4.kicker: § IV · DIALOGUE WITH YOUR EARLIER WORK

p.html: Your note #2204 «The real cost of long windows» from Apr 22 already pointed out: 200K KV cache memory is 25× that of 8K. This week, Lilian Weng's blog4 reaches the same verdict: «the promise of long windows is overstated in production». Your call from 22 days ago is now independently confirmed.

callout.body: «200K KV cache is 25× that of 8K» · Apr 22 · note #2204 — independently supported by Lilian Weng on May 3.

p1.html: Anthropic's rebuttal memo on May 85 argues that RMT v3's «≤ 2.3% compression loss» figure was measured on a narrative-text-biased set. On 1,200 code-completion tasks, the same compressor lost 14.7% in syntactically dense regions. This is the most worth-doubting detail in this week's headline work.

p2.html: The HELM v3 team6 simultaneously argues that needle-in-haystack as an evaluation has become too simple — multi-needle plus counterfactual needles should replace it. So Anthropic's 99.4% figure may itself be re-examined under new evaluation methodology.

share.title: Long-context twins: RMT v3 and Claude 3.5
share.subtitle: Two important works in LLM long-context this week — an editor's excerpt

lede.html: DeepMind's Recurrent Memory Transformer v3 and Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Long-context Eval arrived in the same week, framing two dual paths for long-context research — explicit memory compression on one side, end-to-end attention scaling on the other.

section.s1: § I · Two paths to longer context
section.s3: § III · Dialogue with this reader's prior work

share.p1: RMT v3 maintains linear complexity at 2,097,152 tokens with inference cost just 3.7% of standard attention. Its core mechanism is a 256-token recurrent compression slot folded once every 4,096 tokens.
share.p2: Claude 3.5 hits 99.4% on 200K needle-in-haystack but drops to 73% on the needle-multi-hop subset — exposing the gap between retrieval and reasoning at long context.

claim.1: RMT v3 inference cost is only 3.7% of full attention at 2M tokens
claim.3: Multi-hop accuracy drops to 73%, exposing retrieval-vs-reasoning gap
claim.4: Your 4/17 LongMem note shares the explicit-memory thesis with RMT v3

about.title: A paper edited for one reader.
about.subtitle: Why we built ResearchTrace — and who it's for.

lede.html: ResearchTrace is a proactively-written research paper. It continuously reads what you read, tracks what you track, and every morning before you open it, edits 'what you should know this week' into a paper that is actually readable — evidence-rich, citations clickable.

section.principles: § III · Four things we hold to

mission.headline: Tools should work for you, not the other way around.
mission.p1: Existing notes apps act like warehouses — the more you stack, the further you drift from your library. ResearchTrace inverts this: it actively reads your library and delivers what matters to your desk.
mission.p2: ChatGPT gives you 'plausible-sounding sentences'. ResearchTrace gives you sourced claims. Every conclusion has clickable ① ② ③ — three seconds back to the original.
mission.p3: Research is a periodic activity. We deliver on a daily / weekly / monthly cadence so you can keep up without thinking — that's the real labour-saving.

story.p1: In early 2025, founder Yuwen saved 3,247 links over six months and read just 9% of them. She realised: the problem isn't that she reads too slowly — it's that her tools treat her as a 'warehouse manager' when what she actually needs is a 'newsroom editor'.
story.p2: And so the core idea of ResearchTrace was born: have 5 AI Agents read your library every day, and write a paper for one person — you. The first version went out privately to 14 researchers in September 2025. We've polished the product against their feedback ever since — this paper is, to this day, edited for one reader: you.

p1.v: Every conclusion ships with a clickable citation, three seconds back to the source. No black-box answers.

p2.v: You can see what each Agent did, what it read, and which model it called.

p3.v: End-to-end encrypted, training-immune. Export anytime, no strings.

p4.v: Not a feed — a paper. We respect your attention and only deliver what you need to read today.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.subtitle: Your data is yours. This policy explains how we treat it.

intro.html: Our promise is simple: your data is yours. We do not use your content to train any model, do not share it with third parties, and do not use it for purposes you didn't agree to. This policy explains the specifics.

1.title: 1. What we collect
1.p1: Account information: your email, optional display name, and a hashed password.
1.p2: Your content: PDFs, URLs, emails, Notion items you import — used solely to deliver the Service to you.
1.p3: Usage logs: sign-in time and Agent invocation counts (for billing and ops monitoring) — never any fragment of your content.

2.title: 2. How we use it
2.p1: Your content is used only to (a) parse and extract claims and evidence, (b) write your daily / weekly briefs, (c) answer your ASK queries.
2.p2: We do not: use your content to train any model; share your content with any third party; use it for any purpose not enumerated in this policy without telling you first.

3.title: 3. How we store it
3.p1: Your data is end-to-end encrypted. Storage region: Aliyun Beijing for users in mainland China; AWS us-east-1 for everyone else. Only you hold the decryption key.
3.p2: We snapshot encrypted backups daily on a 30-day rolling window.

4.title: 4. Sharing & disclosure
4.p1: We will not proactively share your data with any third party. Disclosure may occur only when (a) compelled by law, (b) needed to prevent serious bodily harm, or (c) you explicitly authorise it (e.g. by publishing via /share/[id]).
4.p2: Where lawful, we will give you 14 days' notice before any compelled disclosure.

5.title: 5. Your rights
5.p1: You can at any time (a) view and export all your data at /vault, (b) edit account info at /settings, (c) delete your account at /settings (full erasure within 30 days).
5.p2: If your jurisdiction grants additional rights (GDPR, CCPA, etc.), please write to privacy@research.trace to exercise them.

6.title: 6. Cookies & local storage
6.p1: We use the minimum cookies needed to keep you signed in and to remember your language / theme preferences.
6.p2: We do not use third-party tracking cookies. We do not integrate Google Analytics, Facebook Pixel, or any other third-party analytics.

7.title: 7. Minors
7.p1: The Service is intended for users aged 14 and above. We do not knowingly collect data from minors. If you become aware of any such collection, please write to us — we will erase it within 7 days.

8.title: 8. Changes to this policy
8.p1: We may update this policy. Material changes will be announced by email at least 14 days in advance, and the date at the top of this page will be updated.
8.p2: Continued use of the Service constitutes acceptance of the revised policy.

9.title: 9. Contact us
9.p1: For privacy questions, data-rights requests, or complaints, write to privacy@research.trace. We typically reply within 5 business days.
